title: Television in the United States
notes: Cited for: TV first regarded as radio with pictures; in 1948 radio still the number one broadcast medium; four networks (ABC, CBS, NBC, DuMont) and DuMont folding; radio stars reluctant; Berle and Texaco Star Theatre as TV's first hit; under 2 percent of homes with sets at its debut, 70 percent by 1956.

title: CBS Corporation
notes: Cited for: CBS began as a radio network in the late 1920s under William S. Paley; the 1948 talent raid on NBC (Jack Benny, Burns and Allen, Amos 'n' Andy's creators) and the stars' success on TV.

title: Broadcasting
notes: Cited for: advertising became the principal means of support for US broadcasting; sponsored network programs furnished revenue to the network and its stations.

title: The Texaco Star Theatre
notes: Cited for: premiered 1948; Milton Berle as Mr. Television; its live variety show led to a dramatic increase in TV set purchases.

title: Television in the United States: The Kennedy-Nixon debates
notes: Cited for: the first televised presidential debate on September 26, 1960, simulcast on all three networks, about 70 million viewers; nearly 90 percent of homes had TV by 1960.

title: Television in the United States: The era of the miniseries
notes: Cited for: more than 90 percent of the prime-time audience on ABC, CBS or NBC in the late 1970s, 67 percent by 1989; basic cable in 8 percent of homes in 1970, 23 percent in 1980, nearly 60 percent by the end of the 1980s.

title: Television in the United States: The 1990s, the loss of shared experience
notes: Cited for: broadcasting as cultural glue from 1929 to 1989; three-company control of TV produced a unified mass culture that ended in effect in the 1990s; cable services aimed at specific audiences divided viewers.

title: Television in the United States: Early genres
notes: Cited for: anthology dramas (Kraft Television Theatre, Studio One); writers Paddy Chayefsky, Rod Serling, Gore Vidal; Marty (1955) based on a 1953 TV episode and winning best picture.

title: Television in the United States: The late Golden Age
notes: Cited for: most network TV live in 1953 and a minority by 1960; production moving to Los Angeles; filmed shows could earn income indefinitely from reruns.

title: Television in the United States: Sitcoms
notes: Cited for: the sitcom as a 30-minute format with a continuing cast in the same setting; I Love Lucy (CBS, 1951-57) debuted October 1951, shot on film in Hollywood as an episodic series.

title: Television in the United States: CNN
notes: Cited for: CNN began in 1980 and ushered in the era of 24-hour news.

title: Milestones: Ampex Videotape Recorder, 1956
publisher: Engineering and Technology History Wiki (IEEE History Center)
notes: Cited for: before 1956 TV could be recorded only on film, by pointing a movie camera at a monitor (kinescope); poor quality and expense; by 1954 broadcasters used more raw film than the movie industry; Ampex's 1956 videotape recorder replaced kinescopes.

title: 50 Years Ago: Videotape Debuts
notes: Cited for: on November 30, 1956, CBS used an Ampex recorder in Hollywood to tape a live New York newscast and rebroadcast it later to the West Coast; kinescopes as filmed TV screens.

title: I Love Lucy: An American Legend: The Cast, Crew, and Set
notes: Cited for: I Love Lucy adapted from My Favorite Husband; Karl Freund and Marc Daniels generally credited with the three-camera technique before a live audience that became the sitcom standard; the apartment-building setting.

title: We Still Love Lucy (Library of Congress Information Bulletin, September/October 2011)
notes: Cited for: most TV then made in the East and shown to western time zones as kinescopes ('like watching TV through a cheesecloth'); Ball, Arnaz and Oppenheimer chose to produce in Hollywood on 35 mm film before a live audience; My Favorite Husband on CBS radio from 1948; reruns from 1955.

title: Dann Cahn Dead: 'I Love Lucy' Editor, Multicamera Pioneer
notes: Cited for: I Love Lucy used three motion picture cameras and was filmed continuously in sequence like a stage play; editor Dann Cahn cut it on a Moviola with three picture heads and one sound head.

title: Walter Cronkite
notes: Cited for: anchor of the CBS evening news from 1962, when it grew from 15 to 30 minutes, the first half-hour nightly network newscast; 1968 trip to Vietnam after the Tet Offensive and conclusion that the war could end only in stalemate.

title: Vietnam: The Television War (Michael Mandelbaum, Daedalus, Fall 1982)
publisher: American Academy of Arts and Sciences
notes: Cited for: in 1963 the evening national newscasts expanded from 15 minutes to half an hour; Vietnam the first televised war; film of airplanes and troops on patrol; cans of film shipped by air.

title: Quiz Show Scandals
notes: Cited for: accusations in 1958 that quiz shows were rigged and contestants coached; 1959 House hearings; networks leery of single sponsorship afterward, selling time in 15-, 30- and 60-second units.

title: The Aftermath of the Quiz Show Scandal (American Experience)
notes: Cited for: producers took control of shows and stations sold commercial time on the magazine model; removing advertisers from shows ended their urge to interfere; 1960 Communications Act amendments; Walter Lippmann's call for BBC-style TV.

title: A.C. Nielsen Co.
notes: Cited for: TV ratings from 1950 based on a sample of more than 1,000 TV homes with Audimeters, plus diaries; definitions of a rating and a share.

title: Nielsen ratings
notes: Cited for: networks use ratings in part to set advertising rates for each program and to decide which programs to keep or cancel.

title: Remarks Upon Signing the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967 (Lyndon B. Johnson, November 7, 1967)
publisher: The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara
notes: Cited for: signing on November 7, 1967; the Act builds the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, partly government-funded but guarded from government or party control; the Carnegie Commission proposed it; 'what educates can also be exciting'.

title: Public Broadcasting Act of 1967
publisher: American Archive of Public Broadcasting (Library of Congress and GBH)
notes: Cited for: the Act led to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, PBS and NPR.

title: Who Made America? Innovators: Joan Ganz Cooney
notes: Cited for: Cooney founded the Children's Television Workshop in 1968 with Carnegie, Ford and US Commissioner of Education backing; worked with educators and researchers; based the show's fast pace and repeated segments on commercial TV.

title: 'Sesame Street' turns 50
notes: Cited for: the first episode, sponsored by the letters W, S and E and the numbers 2 and 3, aired in fall 1969; designed by educators and child psychologists to help low-income and minority children aged 2 to 5 prepare for school.

title: Sesame Street
notes: Cited for: debuted in 1969 on National Educational Television, which became PBS in 1970; animations, live actors and Jim Henson's Muppets.

title: Cable television
notes: Cited for: US cable systems began in the late 1940s to improve reception in remote and hilly areas; some systems deliver 50 or more channels.

title: HBO
notes: Cited for: started in 1972 with uncut, commercial-free movies for which subscribers paid extra; in 1975 the first American network to deliver programming by satellite, so the first national cable channel.

title: Netflix, Inc.
notes: Cited for: founded 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph as a DVD-rental service ordered online and delivered by mail; streaming introduced in 2007.

title: The Binge Bang Theory (Daniel Frankel)
notes: Cited for: in February 2013 Netflix released all 13 first-season episodes of House of Cards at once; binge viewing predates Netflix (1990s cable marathons, TV on DVD); the next episode queues automatically.

title: Everything Streamed Is New Again
notes: Cited for: viewers embraced having a whole season to watch at their own pace, on whatever screen they wish.

title: Binge-watch (definition)
notes: Cited for: to binge-watch is to watch many or all episodes of a TV series in rapid succession.

title: How Binge-Watching Has Changed TV Writing (Marc Bernardin, guest column)
notes: Cited for: broadcast writers build peril at the end of each act to hold viewers through commercial breaks; binge viewers skip the 'previously on'; writers speak of 'breaking a 10-hour movie'.

title: Broadcasting in the Public Interest: The Newton Minow Collection
publisher: American Archive of Public Broadcasting (Library of Congress and GBH)
notes: Cited for: FCC chairman Newton Minow, appointed by Kennedy in 1961, called commercial TV a 'vast wasteland' in a May 1961 speech to the National Association of Broadcasters; urged the networks to expand nightly news to half an hour; won the Educational Television Facilities Act of 1962, which led toward the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967.
